client:
I just don't understand why I can't seem to enjoy anything anymore. Hiking used to be my favorite thing - I'd go every weekend with my friends. Now when they invite me, I just make excuses because it doesn't feel the same without Maria there. Part of me thinks I should just force myself to go, but what's the point if I'm not going to enjoy it? 

Honestly, I'm skeptical that talking about this will help. It's not like words can magically make me enjoy hiking again. The emptiness is still there whether I talk about it or not.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of loss and longing for the way things used to be, especially with Maria by your side. What if we explored whether the emptiness you feel might be connected not just to missing her, but also to the expectations you have about how hiking "should" feel now? How would it feel to approach hiking as a way to honor those memories, rather than trying to recreate them?

client:
I get what you're saying about honoring the memories instead of trying to recreate them, but it's just... when I'm out there on the trails alone now, it feels like every rock and tree is just reminding me of what I've lost. The idea of hiking feeling different now makes sense logically, but my heart still expects it to feel like it did with her. 

I don't know if I can separate the activity from the loss. Even when I try to think about honoring the memories, it just makes the loneliness sharper. Like I'm carrying this weight that wasn't there before.
therapist: I hear how deeply intertwined your grief is with the hiking experience now, where even the landscape itself seems to echo your loss. It might help to acknowledge that this weight you're carrying is actually a testament to how meaningful those moments with Maria were - the pain exists because the love was real. What would it feel like to let the trail hold both your sorrow and your cherished memories, without needing to choose between them?

client: I get what you're saying about the love and pain being connected, but when I'm actually out there on the trail, all I feel is this crushing emptiness. The memories that used to bring me joy just make me angry now - angry that she's not here to see the views with me anymore. It's like the landscape is mocking me with its beauty.
therapist: It sounds like the anger is protecting you from an even deeper pain - the raw vulnerability of missing her in those beautiful moments you once shared. The landscape isn't just empty now, it's almost painfully alive with what's been lost. What would happen if you let yourself feel that anger fully, rather than trying to push it away or judge it?

client: I don't know if I can let myself feel that anger fully. It scares me because when I start, I'm afraid I won't be able to stop. And then what if all that comes out is just... this bottomless sadness instead? The anger at least makes me feel like I have some control.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd want to hold onto the anger when it feels like the only thing standing between you and overwhelming grief. That fear of being consumed by sadness is very real and valid. What would it look like to explore those feelings in smaller, more manageable moments, rather than all at once?

client: I guess I’ve never thought of it that way—that the anger is almost like a shield. But the idea of letting it go, even in small moments, feels terrifying. What if I can’t handle the sadness underneath? It’s like I’m scared I’ll just fall apart completely if I start to feel it.
therapist: You're describing such an understandable human fear - that if you loosen your grip on the anger, you might drown in the sadness. And yet, I wonder if the parts of you that have carried this grief so far might be stronger than you realize. What would it be like to test that fear gently, perhaps by setting aside just five minutes to feel what's underneath, with the safety of knowing you can return to the anger whenever you need?

client: I get what you're saying, but I'm scared that if I actually let myself feel that sadness, it'll swallow me whole. Five minutes sounds manageable in theory, but what if I can't stop crying once I start? I've spent so much energy staying angry because at least that feels controlled.
therapist: It sounds like you've been carrying this fear that your sadness is bottomless - that if you start crying, you might never stop. Anger has been your emotional anchor, keeping you from feeling adrift in that ocean of grief. What if we explored ways to help you feel safe enough to dip your toes in, like setting a timer or having a comforting ritual afterward?

client: I get what you're saying about anger being my anchor, but that actually makes me feel worse. Like I'm broken for not being able to just grieve normally. The timer idea makes me anxious - what if I can't stop when it goes off? Then I'll have proof that my sadness really is endless.
therapist: It sounds like you're judging yourself harshly for how you're grieving, when in reality there's no "normal" way to process such deep loss. The fear about the timer shows how protective you're being of yourself, which is actually very wise. What if we shifted focus from how you "should" grieve to simply noticing how you're grieving right now, without judgment?

client: I know logically that grief isn't supposed to look a certain way, but I still feel like I'm doing it wrong. When I see other people moving forward while I'm still stuck in this pain, it makes me feel weak or broken. The idea of just observing my grief without judgment sounds impossible - the judgment feels automatic at this point.
therapist: It's understandable that comparison makes your grief feel even heavier, when what you're experiencing is already so painful. Those automatic judgments might actually be part of your grief's voice - a way your mind is trying to make sense of something that feels senseless. What would it be like to notice those judgmental thoughts as just thoughts, rather than truths about who you are?

client: I get what you're saying about the thoughts not being truths, but it's hard not to believe them when they feel so real in the moment. Sometimes when I see other people moving on with their lives, it makes me feel like I'm failing at grieving properly or that I should be "over it" by now. That just makes the loneliness even worse.
therapist: It sounds like those thoughts about "failing" at grief are adding an extra layer of pain to an already difficult experience. The truth is, grief doesn't follow a timeline, and what you're feeling - even the loneliness - is a valid part of your process. What would it feel like to acknowledge that your grief, in all its complexity, is simply a reflection of how deeply you loved and still love Maria?

client: I know logically that grief doesn't have a timeline, but I can't help feeling like I'm stuck when everyone else seems to have moved on. It's been two years since Maria passed, and I still cry at random moments - shouldn't I be "better" by now? The idea that my grief reflects my love makes sense, but it also makes me feel guilty, like my pain is somehow keeping her trapped here with me instead of letting her rest.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying not just grief, but also guilt about how you're grieving - as if your tears are somehow holding Maria back rather than honoring her. That's such a heavy burden to carry. What if we explored whether your tears might actually be a way of continuing to love and remember her, rather than keeping her "trapped"?
